newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Rain lashes central Europe after killer floods.
newsitem.headline: Rain lashes central Europe after killer floods.

text.p: Renewed rains lashed the Czech Republic and Poland, raising river levels perilously high in regions which had yet to recover from earlier devastating flooding.
Heavy rain in the mountains of the northeast Czech Republic turned rivers into raging torrents. A bridge was swept away near the ski resort of Spindleruv Mlyn, Czech Television said.
Several districts were on the highest flood alert and hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes as a precaution.
Severe flooding in the eastern Czech Republic and southern Poland has killed nearly 100 people in the past two weeks but weather forecasters say the rains might ease by Monday.

"Reports...show there is no danger of such a wave (of floods), of such water as we remember a week ago," Polish President Aleksander Kwasnieweski told reporters after a briefing from the national flood crisis committee in Warsaw.
But rains swept across the Czech Republic, raising water levels on already swollen rivers. The heaviest downpour was in the northeastern mountains, where the river Labe rises.

Flood alerts were in force on several rivers, including the Morava and Odra, which flooded last week. Hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes near Jesenik in the northeast as the river Bela rose.
"With the heavier rain, things could worsen during the night," flood commission official Stepan Huzevka told CTK news agency.
Czech authorities had warned on Thursday of a possible new wave of flooding. The first wave, which devastated vast areas of the eastern third of the country, was triggered by days of torrential rain.
At least 45 people were killed as the flood tide destroyed or badly damaged hundreds of homes, cut road, rail and telecommunications links and inundated valuable industrial and crop land.

In Poland, where the first floods killed 49 people, several villages in Zielona Gora province were told to evacuate on Saturday after a dyke broke. Some streets of the lower Silesian mining town of Walbrzych were again under water.

In Opole on the river Odra, where two metres of water raged round high-rise city centre buildings last week, authorities told people to listen for three-minute warning signs, after which they would have an hour to reach evacuation points.

But Polish crisis committeee officials said latest forecasts said the rains were less heavy than first feared. Deputy Environment Minister Krzystof Szamalek said any renewed flooding would be on a scale that could be dealt with, PAP news agency reported.
The rains also put pressure on dykes in eastern Germany, where officials fear they may not stand the strain. Police closed off bridges over the Oder to Poland and evacuated small numbers of people.
